title: Cornwall
capsule: The kingdom of Cornwall emerged from the sub-Roman Brittonic realm of Dumnonia after the Battle of Deorham (577 CE) severed it from Wales, developing a distinct Cornish-speaking Celtic Christian polity in the southwestern peninsula. Cornish forces won the battle at Hehil around 722, likely repelling West Saxon expansion, but the Cornish-Danish alliance was decisively defeated by Æthelstan's predecessor Ecgberht at the Battle of Hingston Down in 838. The last recorded king, Dumgarth, is said to have drowned in 875. Æthelstan (r. 924–939) completed the absorption by fixing the boundary of English settlement at the east bank of the River Tamar around 936, while simultaneously reestablishing a separate Cornish bishop—a measure that preserved ecclesiastical distinctiveness even as political independence ended.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Cornwall's geographic core is well-established; the kingdom's northern and eastern extent during the 8th–9th centuries is only approximately known from place-name evidence and boundary clauses in charters.
